SK2242 The argument check does not run until the result is enumerated

An iterator method validates an argument before its first yield, so the exception is not thrown by the call that passed the bad argument but by whatever later enumerates the result.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS4456

Why

A method containing yield does not run when it is called. The call returns an enumerator and the body starts at the first MoveNext, which means the guard at the top of it — the one written precisely so that a bad argument is rejected early — is the one part of the method guaranteed not to be early. The ArgumentNullException surfaces inside a foreach somewhere else entirely, with a stack trace naming the consumer rather than the caller that broke the contract, and a caller that never enumerates never sees it at all. ⚠ `yield` anywhere in the body makes the whole method lazy, including the statements above the yield, which is what makes this decidable rather than a heuristic: there is no execution in which the guard runs at call time. The repair is the two-method shape — an eager wrapper that validates and returns, and a private iterator that yields.

Example

Instead of:

public IEnumerable<string> Lines(string text) {
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(text);
    foreach (var line in text.Split('\n')) {
        yield return line;
    }
}

Write:

public IEnumerable<string> Lines(string text) {
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(text);
    return LinesCore(text);
}

static IEnumerable<string> LinesCore(string text) {
    foreach (var line in text.Split('\n')) {
        yield return line;
    }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The `async` half of the concept is measured out rather than deferred, and upstream reached the same place. An async method's exception lands on the returned task, which is a real difference — but the overwhelming majority of call sites await the call in the statement that makes it, and there the exception surfaces at exactly the position it would have anyway. SonarQube publishes the two halves separately and puts only the iterator rule, S4456, in its default Sonar way profile; the async rule S4457 is excluded from it. The iterator half is the one where deferral is unconditional, so it is the half that ships. ⚠ Only a check the caller violated is reported, which means a throw of an ArgumentException or one of its subtypes, or a call to a ThrowIf… helper on ArgumentNullException, ArgumentException or ArgumentOutOfRangeException. A method that throws InvalidOperationException before its first yield is describing its own state rather than its caller's mistake, and moving that throw earlier is not obviously right. ⚠ The guard must sit before the first `yield` in source order, because that is what makes it a guard: a throw after a yield is already running inside the enumeration and is where the author put it on purpose. ⚠ A throw inside a `try`, `catch` or `finally` is declined. That is error translation rather than an entry check, and hoisting it out of the handler it sits in would change which exception the caller sees. ⚠ A throw inside a nested lambda or local function is not this method's guard and is skipped, along with the yield statements of any nested local function — those belong to the nested iterator, not to this one. The scan therefore descends the method's own body only. ⚠ `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` iterators are reported too, because the deferral there is the iterator's and not the async machinery's: an async iterator still does not start until something enumerates it, so the guard is deferred for this rule's reason rather than for S4457's. ⚠ Disjoint from `SK3030`, which is about a call site and not a declaration. SK3030 reports an async iterator invoked as a statement and never enumerated; this reports the declaration of an iterator whose guard is deferred. The two register on different node kinds and cannot see the same code. There is no fix: the repair splits one method into two, and the name, the accessibility and the placement of the second are design decisions with no signal in the source — a span edit that guessed them would be a rewrite of a public surface nobody asked for. Generated code is excluded.
